ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> First, the essays were written in response to a minimal, open-ended instruction: participants were asked to write about their thoughts, feelings, and sensations at that moment, as they came to them, continuously and without concern for grammar, sentence structure, or spelling (Pennebaker & King, 1999).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.header: Initial Analysis of Gender Differences in Self-Reported Personality Scores
table.expanded: The model significantly improved over the null model (residual deviance = 2672.9 vs null deviance = 3016.7) and showed acceptable fit (Hosmer-Lemeshow χ 2 (8) = 12.41, p = .134), explaining 19.2% of the variance (Nagelkerke R² ).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .134", Sentence = "The model significantly improved over the null model (residual deviance = 2672.9 vs null deviance = 3016.7) and showed acceptable fit (Hosmer-Lemeshow χ 2 (8) = 12.41, p = .134), explaining 19.2% of the variance (Nagelkerke R² )."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 6 codebook/README/label sources and 93 data columns across 11 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (7 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 2 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: compiled Python files (2). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 93 columns across 11 data files.
#### Issues Identified

8 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 11 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

", "Psychologists. Always trying to understand how the mind works, and how it doesn't work in some cases. Can such things be understood, or are we merely deluding ourselves that knowledge of any kind can be attained?  I guess I've always found psychology to be a very pretentious field. though an interesting one. We all want to control our lives, and anticipating the actions and desires of others helps us maintain that facade of control. Perhaps I'm getting into a more philosophical realm at the moment, but that is where my thoughts take me. Is free will merely an illusion?  I've thought about this a lot. Unfortunately there are no definitive answers to this or other questions. Is there a god?  I've never heard a logically sound argument for the existence of a god. I allow for the possibility of a deity, but it certainly wouldn't be the Christian God. I think ultimately that I have to agree with the existentialists. There is no proof for or against the existence of a god, so we should stop wasting time speculating and just deal with this life. Few people can deal with that. Our fear of death makes us create religions, so that we can pretend there is some semblance of life after our earthly bodies die. These are not new thoughts, I'm just thinking on demand; my mind moves most easily to the pathways it knows, and I present some of the more coherent ideas here. Is someone actually reading this?  Do you understand that I am human?  I am not an object. I am in a body, but I am not the body alone. I am a mind, vast and complex. I am. Do you feel superior because you can analyze minds?  I ask you this, so that you can ask yourself. Do you enjoy treating people as objects?  Do you even admit in your conscious mind that you treat people as objects?  Perhaps not. It's possible that I'm being slightly unfair to you and your profession. Still, it is good to raise questions. We are all just a bit too complacent and easily controlled. I see the need for religion, but I think many of us are above that. I don't need to buy my morality from someone else. What moralists and philosophers do I respect?  Plato, for his logic. Kierkegaard, except the theism. Kant, for his explications of metaphysics and epistemology. Nietzsche, except at the end of his days. LaVey, except for his dependence on rituals and his arrogance. Psychologists and behavioral scientists?  I stay away from most. At some point I'll get back into it, but I was just too turned off by Freud and his pretentious assumptions. Other reading?  Fiction, lots of it. I would name a few dozen authors but then why subject myself to the judgments of someone I can't even see. Music. I find music to be very important. You can't get by without music. And you can't just listen indiscriminately either. I think a real understanding of notes, rhythms, chords, and instrumentation is required before one can say anything about any kind of music. Do you understand music?  How are you reacting to my questions?  You must be used to asking the questions instead of having someone else ask them. Are you getting anything out of this?  Is this more interesting than most responses to the same assignment, or do you even care?  Are you turning to a colleague and saying ""hey, this kid was actually making a futile attempt to understand my motives. ""  Fun with role reversals! ", "Psychologists. Always trying to understand how the mind works, and how it doesn't work in some cases. Can such things be understood, or are we merely deluding ourselves that knowledge of any kind can be attained?  I guess I've always found psychology to be a very pretentious field. though an interesting one. We all want to control our lives, and anticipating the actions and desires of others helps us maintain that facade of control. Perhaps I'm getting into a more philosophical realm at the moment, but that is where my thoughts take me. Is free will merely an illusion?  I've thought about this a lot. Unfortunately there are no definitive answers to this or other questions. Is there a god?  I've never heard a logically sound argument for the existence of a god. I allow for the possibility of a deity, but it certainly wouldn't be the Christian God. I think ultimately that I have to agree with the existentialists. There is no proof for or against the existence of a god, so we should stop wasting time speculating and just deal with this life. Few people can deal with that. Our fear of death makes us create religions, so that we can pretend there is some semblance of life after our earthly bodies die. These are not new thoughts, I'm just thinking on demand; my mind moves most easily to the pathways it knows, and I present some of the more coherent ideas here. Is someone actually reading this?  Do you understand that I am human?  I am not an object. I am in a body, but I am not the body alone. I am a mind, vast and complex. I am. Do you feel superior because you can analyze minds?  I ask you this, so that you can ask yourself. Do you enjoy treating people as objects?  Do you even admit in your conscious mind that you treat people as objects?  Perhaps not. It's possible that I'm being slightly unfair to you and your profession. Still, it is good to raise questions. We are all just a bit too complacent and easily controlled. I see the need for religion, but I think many of us are above that. I don't need to buy my morality from someone else. What moralists and philosophers do I respect?  Plato, for his logic. Kierkegaard, except the theism. Kant, for his explications of metaphysics and epistemology. Nietzsche, except at the end of his days. LaVey, except for his dependence on rituals and his arrogance. Psychologists and behavioral scientists?  I stay away from most. At some point I'll get back into it, but I was just too turned off by Freud and his pretentious assumptions. Other reading?  Fiction, lots of it. I would name a few dozen authors but then why subject myself to the judgments of someone I can't even see. Music. I find music to be very important. You can't get by without music. And you can't just listen indiscriminately either. I think a real understanding of notes, rhythms, chords, and instrumentation is required before one can say anything about any kind of music. Do you understand music?  How are you reacting to my questions?  You must be used to asking the questions instead of having someone else ask them. Are you getting anything out of this?  Is this more interesting than most responses to the same assignment, or do you even care?  Are you turning to a colleague and saying ""hey, this kid was actually making a futile attempt to understand my motives. ""  Fun with role reversals!  I considered producing a surreal and rambling narrative for this assignment, but then you might have taken that a bit too seriously (""bob, we got another wacko here""). Ah well, time passes and other pursuits await. Goodbye for now.  ", "well here I am sitting in front of this glowing monitor trying not to tell the editor in my head overtake me. info.title: The Written Self: Decoding Personality and Gender Differences Through Explainable AI

text.text: This exploratory study examines how gender and personality relate in natural language expression, illustrating how Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques can be used in psychological research.

By analyzing stream-of-consciousness essays from 2,240 undergraduates using BERT with integrated gradients attribution, we identify words and texts that the model relies on to distinguish men's from women's writing, and examine whether they differ across trait levels.
Our approach illustrates how explainability methods can help surface candidate patterns in language use across trait levels and between males and females.
Logistic regression predicting gender from self-reported Big Five scores reveals Neuroticism as the strongest predictor (OR = 2.11, p ≤ .001), followed by Extraversion and Agreeableness.
The BERT model achieves a balanced accuracy of 0.815 in gender classification.

Reading the texts with the highest attribution scores, gender-typical content (e.g., romantic relationships, social affiliation) dominated at both low and high trait levels, alongside a few tentative trait-specific patterns that we offer as hypotheses for future work.
These findings suggest that attribution-guided reading of texts can generate interpretable, testable hypotheses about trait-level patterns in language, complementing traditional methods.
Whether and how men and women differ psychologically remains a question of substantial interest in personality science (Rauthmann & Kuper, 2025).
text.formatted: Whether and how men and women differ psychologically remains a question of substantial interest in personality science <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Rauthmann & Kuper, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analyses have documented gender differences ranging from assertiveness and anxiety (Else-Quest et al., 2006; Feingold, 1994) to the Big Five domains, on which women score higher on average in Neuroticism, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Extraversion (except for its assertiveness facet), and men in Openness, specifically to Ideas (Costa et al., 2001; Kajonius & Johnson, 2018; Lippa, 2010; Vianello et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Meta-analyses have documented gender differences ranging from assertiveness and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Else-Quest et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Feingold, 1994)</ref> to the Big Five domains, on which women score higher on average in Neuroticism, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Extraversion (except for its assertiveness facet), and men in Openness, specifically to Ideas <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Costa et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kajonius & Johnson, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Lippa, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Vianello et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These differences appear across cultures, although the claim that they are larger in more gender-egalitarian countries (Costa et al., 2001; Lippa, 2010; Schmitt et al., 2008) has been challenged by a recent reanalysis, in which the association was attenuated, and sometimes non-significant or even reversed, once cultural region and data quality were taken into account (Berggren & Bergh, 2025).
text.formatted: These differences appear across cultures, although the claim that they are larger in more gender-egalitarian countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Costa et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Lippa, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Schmitt et al., 2008)</ref> has been challenged by a recent reanalysis, in which the association was attenuated, and sometimes non-significant or even reversed, once cultural region and data quality were taken into account <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Berggren & Bergh, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Most of this evidence also rests on global self-reports, which may reflect gender stereotypes and identity as well as how people think, feel, and behave.

In an experience-sampling study, gender differences in emotional stability, agreeableness, and conscientiousness were larger in global trait reports than in average momentary states, where they were not significant, although equivalence could not be established (Buck et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In an experience-sampling study, gender differences in emotional stability, agreeableness, and conscientiousness were larger in global trait reports than in average momentary states, where they were not significant, although equivalence could not be established <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Buck et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: One way to look beyond global self-reports is to examine how traits are expressed.

Language is particularly suited to this, because it is both a behavior and an expression of thoughts and feelings that reveals important aspects of individuals' social and psychological worlds (Pennebaker et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Language is particularly suited to this, because it is both a behavior and an expression of thoughts and feelings that reveals important aspects of individuals' social and psychological worlds <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Pennebaker et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: It has been used to study personality (Park et al., 2014; Schwartz et al., 2013; Tackman et al., 2020) and gender: in a large LIWC-based analysis, women used more words related to social and psychological processes, and men more words referring to objects and impersonal topics (Newman et al., 2008), and metaanalytic evidence shows gender differences in several aspects of language use (Leaper & Ayres, 2007).
text.formatted: It has been used to study personality <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Park et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Schwartz et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al., 2020)</ref> and gender: in a large LIWC-based analysis, women used more words related to social and psychological processes, and men more words referring to objects and impersonal topics <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Newman et al., 2008)</ref>, and metaanalytic evidence shows gender differences in several aspects of language use <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Leaper & Ayres, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Far fewer studies have examined how gender and personality jointly relate to language use, and their results disagree (see Table 1 1 ). Mehl et al. (2006) used Electronically Activated Recorders (EAR) to sample spontaneous spoken language in daily life and found significant differences between men and women in how personality traits showed up in behavior.

text.text: A later study with a larger and more diverse sample (462 compared to the original 96 participants) found few such differences: only 5% of trait-behavior correlations (31 of 620) differed significantly between men and women (Tackman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: A later study with a larger and more diverse sample (462 compared to the original 96 participants) found few such differences: only 5% of trait-behavior correlations (31 of 620) differed significantly between men and women <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Tackman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Estimates are imprecise even for a simpler measure: in a preregistered replication of Mehl et al. (2007) pooling 22 samples (N = 2,197), Tidwell et al. (2025) found a small gender difference in the number of words spoken per day (d = 0.13), but the estimate was too imprecise to establish either equivalence or a meaningful difference.

(2025)</ref> found a small gender difference in the number of words spoken per day (d = 0.13), but the estimate was too imprecise to establish either equivalence or a meaningful difference.

text.text: Part of this disagreement may arise because gender differences in language are not consistent across trait levels: individuals with low or high trait scores might show different patterns from those at moderate levels (Hofmann et al., 2025; Tackman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Part of this disagreement may arise because gender differences in language are not consistent across trait levels: individuals with low or high trait scores might show different patterns from those at moderate levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hofmann et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, women typically score higher on Neuroticism than men, yet Tackman et al. (2020) found that higher Neuroticism was associated with more sadness-related words among women but not among men.
text.formatted: For instance, women typically score higher on Neuroticism than men, yet <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al. (2020)</ref> found that higher Neuroticism was associated with more sadness-related words among women but not among men.

text.text: Two complementary theoretical frameworks motivate examining such variation.

First, Whole Trait Theory (WTT) proposes that personality traits are density distributions of states rather than fixed characteristics, with the expression of traits varying across moments and contexts through social-cognitive mechanisms (Fleeson & Jayawickreme, 2015).
text.formatted: First, Whole Trait Theory (WTT) proposes that personality traits are density distributions of states rather than fixed characteristics, with the expression of traits varying across moments and contexts through social-cognitive mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Fleeson & Jayawickreme, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: WTT was developed to account for within-person situational variability, but its central insight, that identical trait levels can produce different behavioral expressions depending on individual characteristics, can be extended to stable characteristics such as gender.
Men and women with similar trait levels may then enact those traits differently in language.

Second, research on person-situation interactions has documented individual differences in how people respond to situational characteristics, and these contingencies between situation characteristics and personality states are themselves important individual difference variables (Kuper et al., 2022 (Kuper et al., , 2024)).
text.formatted: Second, research on person-situation interactions has documented individual differences in how people respond to situational characteristics, and these contingencies between situation characteristics and personality states are themselves important individual difference variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kuper et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Kuper et al., , 2024))</ref>.

text.text: People also perceive identical situations differently, and this idiosyncratic variance depends on characteristics such as personality traits and demographic factors, including gender (Horstmann et al., 2021).
text.formatted: People also perceive identical situations differently, and this idiosyncratic variance depends on characteristics such as personality traits and demographic factors, including gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Horstmann et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Extending this framework to verbal expression, gender differences in language use may vary systematically across personality trait levels.
Studying such variation requires methods that can capture it.
Language analysis in psychology has moved from word counting toward context-sensitive representations (Boyd & Schwartz, 2021).
text.formatted: Language analysis in psychology has moved from word counting toward context-sensitive representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Boyd & Schwartz, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Closed-vocabulary methods such as the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) count words in predefined categories, whereas open-vocabulary methods such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) derive categories from the texts themselves (Eichstaedt et al., 2021; Park et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Closed-vocabulary methods such as the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) count words in predefined categories, whereas open-vocabulary methods such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) derive categories from the texts themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Eichstaedt et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Park et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Both have yielded many findings into personality and gender (Park et al., 2014 (Park et al., , 2016;; Schwartz et al., 2013; Tackman et al., 2020), but both treat words or topics as isolated units: a dictionary counts "bank" identically whether it refers to a financial institution or a riverbank.
text.formatted: Both have yielded many findings into personality and gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Park et al., 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Park et al., , 2016;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Schwartz et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al., 2020</ref>), but both treat words or topics as isolated units: a dictionary counts "bank" identically whether it refers to a financial institution or a riverbank.

text.text: They may therefore miss subtler differences in how men and women express the same trait.

Transformer models such as BERT (Rogers et al., 2020; Vaswani et al., 2017) build contextualized representations, in which the same word is represented differently depending on its surroundings (see Materials and Methods).
text.formatted: Transformer models such as BERT <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Rogers et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Vaswani et al., 2017)</ref> build contextualized representations, in which the same word is represented differently depending on its surroundings (see Materials and Methods).

text.text: In psychology, they have been used to improve the prediction of personality traits and to revisit aspects of the lexical hypothesis (Saeteros et al., 2025)  (Cutler & Condon, 2022).
text.formatted: In psychology, they have been used to improve the prediction of personality traits and to revisit aspects of the lexical hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Saeteros et al., 2025)</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cutler & Condon, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These capabilities do not replace psychological theory, which is still needed to interpret what the models detect.
Models used only to maximize prediction accuracy can show that language carries trait-related signal, but not why, or for whom.

Moving from prediction toward understanding requires interpreting model outputs within personality theory and considering how verbal expression interacts with situational contexts (e.g., assessment settings, communication media) and with other psychological variables, such as gender (Boyd & Markowitz, 2024).
text.formatted: Moving from prediction toward understanding requires interpreting model outputs within personality theory and considering how verbal expression interacts with situational contexts (e.g., assessment settings, communication media) and with other psychological variables, such as gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Boyd & Markowitz, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such integration could also help the field build explanatory accounts of trait expression on a descriptive foundation (Boyd & Pennebaker, 2017).
text.formatted: Such integration could also help the field build explanatory accounts of trait expression on a descriptive foundation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Boyd & Pennebaker, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: XAI offers a practical route toward this integration.

By identifying which linguistic features contribute most to a model's predictions, it shows how patterns vary across trait levels or between groups, and links trait scores to specific words and texts.
This contribution is, at first, descriptive: it specifies which words co-occur with which trait levels, in which gender, and in which contexts.
Such descriptive findings are the material from which explanatory accounts can later be built (Mõttus et al., 2020), because they define what theories of trait expression must account for.
text.formatted: Such descriptive findings are the material from which explanatory accounts can later be built <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Mõttus et al., 2020)</ref>, because they define what theories of trait expression must account for.

text.text: To our knowledge, contextual models with XAI have not yet been used to study how gender differences in language vary across trait levels.

We adopt an exploratory, hypothesis-generating design, following the approach of (Saeteros et al., 2025): a BERT classifier trained to distinguish men's from women's essays, whose predictions are inspected with integrated gradients.
text.formatted: We adopt an exploratory, hypothesis-generating design, following the approach of <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Saeteros et al., 2025)</ref>: a BERT classifier trained to distinguish men's from women's essays, whose predictions are inspected with integrated gradients.

text.text: Integrated gradients show which words drive each prediction, so that the detected patterns can be read and interpreted, following an approach recently discussed for psychology in the context of correlations (Mõttus, 2022).
text.formatted: Integrated gradients show which words drive each prediction, so that the detected patterns can be read and interpreted, following an approach recently discussed for psychology in the context of correlations <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Mõttus, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: We intend it as a step toward explanatory accounts, generating specific, testable patterns that later work can examine with designs capable of addressing mechanisms, such as prompted-topic writing tasks, experience sampling combined with language data (Buck et al., 2026), or preregistered confirmatory tests on independent corpora.
text.formatted: We intend it as a step toward explanatory accounts, generating specific, testable patterns that later work can examine with designs capable of addressing mechanisms, such as prompted-topic writing tasks, experience sampling combined with language data <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Buck et al., 2026)</ref>, or preregistered confirmatory tests on independent corpora.

text.text: We ask (1) how men's and women's language use differs overall, and (2) how it differs between men and women who share similar trait levels, with particular attention to the lowest and highest quartiles of each trait.
Our study followed a workflow similar to that of Saeteros et al. (2025), organized in three phases (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Our study followed a workflow similar to that of <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Saeteros et al. (2025)</ref>, organized in three phases (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: In Phase 1, the essays were split into fragments and the personality scores were standardized.

In Phase 2, we conducted two preliminary analyses of the personality scores and two language analyses: the log-odds ratio with Informative Dirichlet Prior (IDP), and the attribution of the predictions of a BERT gender classifier using integrated gradients.
In Phase 3, the outputs of the language analyses were used to identify and interpret the linguistic patterns that characterize each gender.
Both language analyses were conducted under two aspects.

The Gender Only aspect examined gender differences in language use regardless of personality, whereas the Gender and Personality aspect compared males and females within extreme trait groups (e.g., females with high Agreeableness scores vs. males with high Agreeableness scores), following an approach similar to that of Mõttus (2022) but using quartiles instead of tertiles.
text.formatted: The Gender Only aspect examined gender differences in language use regardless of personality, whereas the Gender and Personality aspect compared males and females within extreme trait groups (e.g., females with high Agreeableness scores vs. males with high Agreeableness scores), following an approach similar to that of <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Mõttus (2022)</ref> but using quartiles instead of tertiles.

text.text: Quartiles were computed on the year-standardized z-scores of each trait: low trait groups (Q1) comprised participants at or below the 25th percentile and high trait groups (Q4) those above the 75th percentile.

For the log-odds analysis, cut-offs were computed on the whole sample, so that men and women in each group had the same absolute trait level; for the attribution analysis, they were computed separately for males and females, so that each gender contributed a comparable number of texts to the selection of high-attribution words.
The classifier was trained to predict gender, not personality.
Its attribution scores therefore identify what distinguishes men's from women's writing, and trait information enters only through the stratification of participants into low and high trait groups.
We do not infer personality traits from vocabulary.

We used the Essays dataset (Pennebaker & King, 1999), which contains 2,240 streamof-consciousness essays (1,342 females and 898 males) written freely for 20 minutes by undergraduate students between 1997 and 2004foot_1 .
text.formatted: We used the Essays dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Pennebaker & King, 1999)</ref>, which contains 2,240 streamof-consciousness essays (1,342 females and 898 males) written freely for 20 minutes by undergraduate students between 1997 and 2004<ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref> .

text.text: We chose it for two reasons.

First, the essays were written in response to a minimal, open-ended instruction: participants were asked to write about their thoughts, feelings, and sensations at that moment, as they came to them, continuously and without concern for grammar, sentence structure, or spelling (Pennebaker & King, 1999).
text.formatted: First, the essays were written in response to a minimal, open-ended instruction: participants were asked to write about their thoughts, feelings, and sensations at that moment, as they came to them, continuously and without concern for grammar, sentence structure, or spelling <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Pennebaker & King, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Topic and style were therefore not imposed by a platform or an audience, and the texts may reflect thoughts and feelings more than conversational behavior shaped by an interlocutor or setting.

Second, every participant also completed a 44-item Big Five Inventory (John et al., 1991) in a version with simplified item wording, and the corpus is, to our knowledge, one of the most widely studied datasets pairing free text with Big Five scores (Mairesse et al., 2007), which allows our results to be compared with a large body of prior work.
text.formatted: Second, every participant also completed a 44-item Big Five Inventory <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(John et al., 1991)</ref> in a version with simplified item wording, and the corpus is, to our knowledge, one of the most widely studied datasets pairing free text with Big Five scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Mairesse et al., 2007)</ref>, which allows our results to be compared with a large body of prior work.

text.text: Its main limitations are its age and the assigned academic writing context (see Limitations).

Other corpora with Big Five scores exist: myPersonality, built on Facebook, is no longer available (Stillwell & Kosinski, 2015), and PANDORA, built on Reddit (Gjurković et al., 2021), is left for future work.
text.formatted: Other corpora with Big Five scores exist: myPersonality, built on Facebook, is no longer available <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Stillwell & Kosinski, 2015)</ref>, and PANDORA, built on Reddit <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gjurković et al., 2021)</ref>, is left for future work.

text.text: Because our dataset's "sex" variable was self-reported, we interpret it as reflecting gender identity rather than biological sex (American Psychological Association, 2020, Section 5.5) and use the term gender throughout, while acknowledging that the dataset does not capture gender beyond this binary classification.
Likewise, "trait" and "trait level" refer throughout to scores on the self-report Big Five inventory, not to an underlying disposition.
Since the inventory was scored differently across years (sum scores in some years, mean scores in others), personality scores were standardized within each year using z-scores.
Because the essays exceeded BERT's 512-token limit, they were divided into 256-word fragments, each of which inherited the gender label of its essay.
As a preliminary validation step, we computed Cohen's d effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals for each trait and fitted a logistic regression predicting gender from the five traits.
These analyses check that the sample reproduces the gender differences in personality reported in previous research before we turn to language.
The log-odds ratio with IDP (Monroe et al., 2008) identifies words whose usage frequency differs between groups.
text.formatted: The log-odds ratio with IDP <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Monroe et al., 2008)</ref> identifies words whose usage frequency differs between groups.

text.text: It compares the odds of each word in the two groups, which accounts for differences in corpus size, and uses an informative Dirichlet prior given by the combined word counts of the two groups being compared, which shrinks estimates for rare words toward their overall frequency.
The resulting z-scores are positive for greater female usage and negative for greater male usage.
Two-sided p-values were adjusted with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) over the vocabulary of each comparison, with q < .05 as the significance criterion.
text.formatted: Two-sided p-values were adjusted with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)</ref> over the vocabulary of each comparison, with q < .05 as the significance criterion.

text.text: We computed z-scores for the whole sample (Gender Only aspect) and within the Q1 and Q4 groups of each trait (Gender and Personality aspect).
In addition, a two-proportion z-test compared the proportion of males using "girlfriend" with the proportion of females using "boyfriend".
We fine-tuned BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), a language model based on the transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017).
text.formatted: We fine-tuned BERT <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Devlin et al., 2019)</ref>, a language model based on the transformer architecture <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Vaswani et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Transformers are neural networks built around an attention mechanism, which allows the model to weigh, for each word, how relevant every other word in the text is to its interpretation.
BERT was pre-trained on large text corpora.
Pre-training provides the model with general knowledge of language structure and meaning, which fine-tuning then adapts to a specific task with far less labelled data than training from scratch.
BERT splits text into subword tokens and, by stacking several attention layers, builds a representation of each token that takes into account both its left and right context.
As a result, unlike word-counting approaches, the same word can contribute differently to a prediction depending on how it is used.
In this study, BERT was fine-tuned to predict the author's gender from each fragment.
Performance was evaluated at the fragment level with the balanced accuracy (the mean of sensitivity and specificity, robust to class imbalance).

The fragments were randomly partitioned into training (90%) and test (10%) sets, and 10% of the training set was held out as a validation set to select the best training epoch (see Implementation Details).
To identify the words driving the model's predictions, we applied integrated gradients (Sundararajan et al., 2017) to the test set fragments.
text.formatted: To identify the words driving the model's predictions, we applied integrated gradients <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Sundararajan et al., 2017)</ref> to the test set fragments.

text.text: This method integrates the model's gradients along a path from a baseline input to the actual input, assigning each token a score that indicates whether it increased (positive score) or decreased (negative score) the probability of the predicted class.
Token scores are summed to obtain a text-level score for the whole fragment.
Since attributions are assigned to the subword tokens of the BERT tokenizer, each token was treated as a unit of analysis, which we refer to as a word for simplicity.

Following Saeteros et al. (2025), within the fragments predicted as each gender, we separated positive attributions (supporting the predicted class) from negative attributions (supporting the opposite class), so that, for instance, a negative attribution in a fragment predicted as female was taken as evidence for the male class.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Saeteros et al. (2025)</ref>, within the fragments predicted as each gender, we separated positive attributions (supporting the predicted class) from negative attributions (supporting the opposite class), so that, for instance, a negative attribution in a fragment predicted as female was taken as evidence for the male class.

text.text: We then applied the maximum attribution technique, which keeps the highest absolute score of each word across all its occurrences, and visualized these scores with bar plots and word clouds (Halvey & Keane, 2007).
text.formatted: We then applied the maximum attribution technique, which keeps the highest absolute score of each word across all its occurrences, and visualized these scores with bar plots and word clouds <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Halvey & Keane, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Only correctly classified fragments, and words appearing at least 10 times in them, were considered.
The same model was used for both aspects: attributions for the Gender and Personality aspect were obtained by filtering the test fragments by gender and trait quartile.
Two additional checks addressed potential shortcuts in the model.

First, to assess the influence of obvious gender-identifying terms, we trained the model on a version of the data in which relationship terms ("boyfriend", "girlfriend", and their variants) were masked.

Second, because our aim was to characterize gender-linked language rather than to build a classifier, the data were split at the fragment level, so that the full content of every essay contributed to the analysis; consequently, fragments from the same essay may appear in different partitions, which could lead the model to rely on author-specific cues.
However, the top-ranked attribution words (Figure 3) were not author-specific: each appeared in at least 45 different essays, and no single essay accounted for more than 8% of its occurrences.
text.formatted: However, the top-ranked attribution words (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>) were not author-specific: each appeared in at least 45 different essays, and no single essay accounted for more than 8% of its occurrences.

text.text: Moreover, with an author-level split, balanced accuracy decreased only slightly (0.797 vs.
0.815), as expected given the small number of fragments per essay (median = 3).
In Phase 3, the log-odds z-scores identified words with greater female or male usage, either in the whole sample or within each trait quartile.
The attribution scores were used to select the fragments to be examined, so that selection relied on the model rather than on researcher choice.

For each gender, we took the five words with the highest maximum attribution scores and, for each of them, examined the 10 fragments in which the word reached its highest attribution score and the 10 fragments containing the word with the highest text-level attribution scores.
In the Gender Only aspect, we additionally examined, for each gender, the 10 fragments with the highest text-level attribution scores.
The Gender and Personality aspect applied the same word-level procedure within each combination of gender, trait, and quartile (e.g., female-Q1-Agreeableness).
Interpretation followed two steps.

First, the selected words and fragments of each group were read and compared with previous findings, particularly Tackman et al. (2020), Newman et al. (2008), and Mehl et al. (2006), to identify documented linguistic markers of personality and gender.
text.formatted: First, the selected words and fragments of each group were read and compared with previous findings, particularly <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al. (2020)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Newman et al. (2008)</ref>, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Mehl et al. (2006)</ref>, to identify documented linguistic markers of personality and gender.

text.text: Second, the same outputs were reviewed for gender-specific patterns not previously documented.
Reading was done without a predefined coding scheme or counts; keyword searches within the selected fragments served only to locate examples.
Across all groups, the selection yielded 327 unique fragments (180 female, 147 male), and the same fragment can be selected in more than one group.
Excerpts reported in the Results and Tables were checked against the source fragments and lightly normalized (capitalization and spacing).
Although selection was algorithm-driven, interpretation involves theoretical framing and researcher judgment; the examples therefore serve as illustrations.

We fine-tuned the "bert-base-uncased" version of BERT with the Hugging Face Transformers library (Wolf et al., 2020) for PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019), tokenizing the fragments with the BERT tokenizer from the same library.
text.formatted: We fine-tuned the "bert-base-uncased" version of BERT with the Hugging Face Transformers library <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Wolf et al., 2020)</ref> for PyTorch <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Paszke et al., 2019)</ref>, tokenizing the fragments with the BERT tokenizer from the same library.

text.text: The model was trained for three epochs with a batch size of 16, a learning rate of 4 × 10 -5 , a hidden dropout probability of 0.1, and an attention dropout probability of 0.2.
After each epoch, we evaluated the model on the validation set and kept the checkpoint with the highest validation balanced accuracy.
Attribution scores were computed with the Transformers Interpret library 3 , which provides an integrated gradients implementation for transformers.

This library applies a zero-embedding vector as the default reference baseline for integrated gradients, that is, a reference input in which all token embeddings are set to zero, representing the absence of any linguistic signal.

This is a standard choice that satisfies the completeness property of integrated gradients, ensuring that attribution scores account for the full difference between the model's output on the actual text and on the empty baseline (Sundararajan et al., 2017); attribution scores are therefore interpretable relative to this baseline.
text.formatted: This is a standard choice that satisfies the completeness property of integrated gradients, ensuring that attribution scores account for the full difference between the model's output on the actual text and on the empty baseline <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Sundararajan et al., 2017)</ref>; attribution scores are therefore interpretable relative to this baseline.

text.text: Initial analyses examined basic gender differences in personality traits using standardized scores.
Cohen's d effect sizes revealed significant differences between males and females across all Big Five traits (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: Cohen's d effect sizes revealed significant differences between males and females across all Big Five traits (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Females scored higher in Neuroticism (d = -0.45, [-0.53, -0.36]), Extraversion (d = -0.32, [-0.41, -0.24]), Agreeableness (d = -0.32, [-0.40, -0.23]), and Conscientiousness (d = -0.25, [-0.34, -0.17]).
Males scored higher only in Openness to Experience, with a small effect (d = 0.17, [0.08, 0.25]).
All effects were statistically significant based on 95% confidence intervals.
A logistic regression predicting gender from personality traits found all Big Five traits were significant predictors (p ≤ .001), with a balanced accuracy of 0.724.
Neuroticism was the strongest predictor (OR = 2.11), followed by Extraversion (OR = 1.58) and Agreeableness (OR = 1.49).
Conscientiousness showed a moderate effect (OR = 1.28), while Openness to Experience demonstrated an inverse relationship (OR = 0.83).

The model significantly improved over the null model (residual deviance = 2672.9 vs null deviance = 3016.7) and showed acceptable fit (Hosmer-Lemeshow χ 2 (8) = 12.41, p = .134), explaining 19.2% of the variance (Nagelkerke R² ).
The BERT model achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.815 in classifying text segments by author gender.

Two complementary analyses identify linguistic patterns that differ between males and females: a log-odds ratio analysis, whose z-scores are reported in Table 2, and word attribution scores from the classifier, presented in the explainability sections below.
text.formatted: Two complementary analyses identify linguistic patterns that differ between males and females: a log-odds ratio analysis, whose z-scores are reported in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref>, and word attribution scores from the classifier, presented in the explainability sections below.

text.text: Because "girlfriend" and "boyfriend" have gendered referents, gendered use of these terms is expected.
A two-proportion z-test comparing "girlfriend" usage among males (234/898 = 26.1%) versus "boyfriend" usage among females (404/1342 = 30.1%), yielded a significant difference (z = -2.08, p = .037).
Moreover, validation experiments using masked versions of these terms showed minimal impact on classification performance (balanced accuracy = 0.808 vs.
0.815, masked and original, respectively), suggesting that classification does not depend on them.
Log-odds ratio with IDP analysis identified 21 words with significant gender associations after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q < .05).
text.formatted: Log-odds ratio with IDP analysis identified 21 words with significant gender associations after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q < .05).

text.text: Males showed stronger associations with activity terms (Newman et al., 2008; Park et al., 2016) ("play", "playing", "game", "music"), while females showed stronger associations with social-life terms (Newman et al., 2008; Park et al., 2016) ("sorority"), familial references (Newman et al., 2008) ("mom"), and the intensive adverb "really" (Park et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Males showed stronger associations with activity terms <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Newman et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Park et al., 2016)</ref> ("play", "playing", "game", "music"), while females showed stronger associations with social-life terms <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Newman et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Park et al., 2016)</ref> ("sorority"), familial references <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Newman et al., 2008)</ref> ("mom"), and the intensive adverb "really" <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Park et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Relationship terms ("girlfriend" for males, "boyfriend" for females) were also among these words, as expected given their gendered referents (see above).
Complete results are presented in Table 2.
text.formatted: Complete results are presented in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref>.

text.text: Analysis of word attribution scores identified gender-specific language patterns.
Using the maximum score summarization technique, we identified words with the strongest influence on gender classification (see Figure 4).
text.formatted: Using the maximum score summarization technique, we identified words with the strongest influence on gender classification (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: For males, the highest attribution scores were for "girlfriend", "love", "roommate", "stream", and "band" (see Figure 3).
text.formatted: For males, the highest attribution scores were for "girlfriend", "love", "roommate", "stream", and "band" (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>).

text.text: Inspection of the underlying texts showed that the word itself presented small attribution scores for "love", "roommate", and "stream", and that their selection mainly reflects the surrounding essay, whereas "girlfriend" and "band" presented larger positive word-level scores.
"Stream" in particular mostly comes from references to the writing task ("stream of consciousness") rather than from gendered content.

The male list therefore points to romantic relationships and music more clearly than to social or leisure themes.  (a) Female-associated linguistic patterns (b) Male-associated linguistic patterns For females, the highest attribution scores were for "boyfriend", "sorority", "cute", "girl", and "dance".

These words were consistently highlighted in the texts, and they point to romantic relationships, social affiliations, and positive evaluations ("cute" was mostly used for boys and children), with "dance" referring to dance performance and events.
"Girl" occurred both in self-reference and in references to other girls (see Figure 3).
text.formatted: "Girl" occurred both in self-reference and in references to other girls (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>).

text.text: The following analysis is based on text segments selected through the attribution-score procedure described in Phase 3: Selection and Interpretation of Attribution Outputs.

The examples come from a limited number of essays, were not systematically coded, and serve as illustrations only; the full attribution outputs are available on the https://osf.io/5xz7w/?view_only=2a4174722b2e4a7aa38e83bafa031a37.
text.formatted: The examples come from a limited number of essays, were not systematically coded, and serve as illustrations only; the full attribution outputs are available on the <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/5xz7w/?view_only=2a4174722b2e4a7aa38e83bafa031a37">OSF</ref>.

text.text: In the high-scoring texts, we could not identify clear differences in writing style between male and female authors.

Both genders disclosed emotions directly (females: "I feel really sad because I miss my family so bad"; males: "my biggest fear is never seeing my friends again") and both weighed options in practical terms (females: "which is more important?
I guess more things will come up in the evenings than in the mornings"; males: "that would be very time consuming...
I will have a lot to do besides"), and in both genders we found fragmented, topic-jumping texts as well as connected narratives.

The differences we could identify concerned topical content, in line with the word-level results: for example, leisure activities such as dance for females ("I love to dance also, and I can't wait to try out for pom squad") and music for males ("I am listening to some audio adrenaline. they are a christian band I just downloaded").

Contrast constructions appeared in both genders, with somewhat different content: some male fragments used them for intellectual contrast ("although, in class you said…", "in general, not every woman"), whereas some female fragments used them around emotional and interpersonal concerns ("if only I could help him… but I know time is all he needs", "I am content… but I do miss").

Explicit sexual references appeared mainly in male texts ("thinking back to short, white hair and anonymous breasts", "she was drunk on our first date, she'd been with many other partners"), while the female relationship-focused fragments contained little explicit sexual language.
This analysis asks which words distinguish men and women within the lowest (Q1) and highest (Q4) quartile of each trait.
Each z-score compares men's and women's use of a word within the same quartile (negative values indicate male-associated words); it does not compare Q1 with Q4 within a gender.

Because men contributed about half as much text in Q4 as in Q1 and the difference between quartiles was not tested, we do not take this contrast as evidence that the gender difference varies with trait level.
All other listed words, including activity terms such as "playing" (among the top male-associated words in Q1 of four traits), did not survive correction and are reported as tentative.
For women, "boyfriend" had its highest z-scores in Agreeableness Q1 (z = 2.45), Extraversion Q1 (z = 2.33), and Neuroticism Q1 (z = 2.10).
For men, "girlfriend" had its highest z-scores in Openness Q1 (z = -2.60), Neuroticism Q4 (z = -2.33), Conscientiousness Q4 (z = -2.25), and Agreeableness Q1 (z = -2.24).

The size of the male-female contrast in these terms differed numerically between quartiles (e.g., in Openness, "girlfriend" z = -2.60 in Q1 vs -2.07 in Q4; "boyfriend" z = 2.07 in Q1 vs 1.62 in Q4), but we did not test whether these differences are reliable.
Across the ten trait-quartile groups, the words with the highest attribution were largely the same in Q1 and Q4 and were dominated by gender-typical content.

For females, "boyfriend" was among the two top words in every group, with consistently high word-level attribution scores (mean scores of about 0.7-0.9), followed by words such as "girl", "love", "cute", and "sorority".

For males, the words were more heterogeneous and their wordlevel attribution scores were mostly lower (below 0.2 on average, with "girlfriend" as the exception), so their selection partly reflects the surrounding essay.
Trait-related differences between quartiles were limited and are described below as tentative observations.

At lower Openness levels (Q1), males' top words were leisure and activity terms ("music", "college", "football"), where "football" falls within the sports category that men used more in Newman et al. (2008), and females' were "sorority" and "boyfriend", words that point to social affiliation and relationships (Newman et al., 2008; Park et al., 2016).

text.text: Conscientiousness.

At lower Conscientiousness levels (Q1), the male words ("though", "good", "first") were function words and general evaluatives with small wordlevel scores, so no content theme could be identified, while the female words were relational terms ("boyfriend", "girl", "someone").
At higher Conscientiousness levels (Q4), the male words were "girlfriend", "music", and "football" and the female words were "boyfriend", "cute", and "love".
In neither quartile did the highlighted words refer to content related to the trait (e.g., planning or organization).
Extraversion.

At lower Extraversion levels (Q1), males' top words were "music", "college", and "kind", the latter almost always in the hedge "kind of" (e.g., "i am kind of worried"), while females' were "boyfriend", "cute", "girl", and "hate", which mostly expressed dislike of tasks and things (e.g., reading, tests, weight) and not of people.

At higher Extraversion levels (Q4), males' top words were "love", "girl", and "talk", mostly in contexts of romantic interest (e.g., "I'd like to talk to her", "I still love her"), while females' were "sorority" and "roommate", which refer to social organizations and shared living contexts (Park et al., 2016).
text.formatted: At higher Extraversion levels (Q4), males' top words were "love", "girl", and "talk", mostly in contexts of romantic interest (e.g., "I'd like to talk to her", "I still love her"), while females' were "sorority" and "roommate", which refer to social organizations and shared living contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Park et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In both genders the Q4 words refer somewhat more to social contact than the Q1 words, although the differences are small.
Agreeableness.

At lower Agreeableness levels (Q1), "girlfriend" was the male word with the most consistent word-level scores and appeared in contexts of current and former partners (e.g., "my ex-girlfriend from high school came in", "I wish I was at home with my girlfriend"), together with "music" and "college".
Females' top words were relational terms ("boyfriend", "girl", "love") together with "hate", used in the same way as in Extraversion Q1.

At higher Agreeableness levels (Q4), the male words ("girl", "talk", "love") appeared in contexts of attraction to or approaching a girl (e.g., "the girl I like will be there"), and "stream" mostly comes from references to the writing task.
Females' words were "love", "miss", and "sister" (e.g., "right now I miss him.
I feel love and sorrow"), which are affectionate terms, in line with the small female advantage in affiliative speech (Leaper & Ayres, 2007).
text.formatted: I feel love and sorrow"), which are affectionate terms, in line with the small female advantage in affiliative speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Leaper & Ayres, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: We found no link between the contexts of the male words and Agreeableness itself.
Neuroticism.

At lower Neuroticism levels (Q1), males' top words were "stream" (from the writing task), "girl" (with low and inconsistent word-level scores), and "music", while females' were relational terms ("boyfriend", "girl", "love").
At higher Neuroticism levels (Q4), males' words included "play", "college", "damn", and "though".

"Damn" appeared in mild exclamations and complaints (e.g., "damn, I'm so freaking superficial", "this damn class") and swear words were used more by men in Newman et al. (2008), and "though" appeared in contexts such as "I miss her though".

text.text: Females' words in Q4 were "boyfriend", "girl", "cute", and "love".
Female words were similar in both quartiles, and male words varied more but with low word-level scores.
We read the high-scoring essay fragments of each trait-quartile group against the general disposition described by each Big Five trait and the items of the Big Five Inventory.
Across the ten groups, the texts were dominated by the gender-typical content already described and by everyday concerns of undergraduate students, which appeared in both quartiles of every trait.

Differences between low (Q1) and high (Q4) trait levels were visible only in some groups and are described here as tentative impressions, each based on a small number of fragments; example excerpts are lightly normalized (capitalization and spacing).

For Openness, high-scoring men wrote more abstract and existential texts ("god is just santa clause for adults"; "we are all one consciousness functioning at different levels"), while we found no pattern in women.

For Conscientiousness, low-scoring men described laziness and distractibility ("I could quite possibly be the laziest person on this earth"; "I have always had a problem with being too easily distracted"), while high-scoring men more often referred to completing or preparing work ("I have just finished the rough draft of my rhetoric paper"; "maybe I will take a nap, except I have to study"); we found no such contrast in women, whose Q4 texts also included procrastination ("I was just looking for an excuse to put off my reading").

For Extraversion, low-scoring women more often described shyness or loneliness ("I have never really been one to mingle in a crowd"; "lately I have been feeling lonely, very lonely"), whereas we found no clear pattern in men.

For Agreeableness, annoyance and criticism of others appeared in both quartiles of both genders (e.g., "it annoys me to no extent when people don't keep up with it", female Q4), so we could not identify differences by trait level.

For Neuroticism, texts of both genders in Q1 often paired distress with positive reappraisal ("besides the occasional loneliness, I am very happy with my new life here at college", male; "other than feeling really tired and lazy, I am also feeling happy", female), whereas Q4 texts more often stated worry or irritation without such reappraisal ("I've always had so much to do that when I don't, I can't relax and I get really anxious", female; "if we're friends then why do I find myself mad at her all the time", male).
Distress was also present in Q1 texts.
Verbatim excerpts for each impression are given in Table 4, and Table 5 summarizes the word-level and whole-text results by trait and quartile.

text.text: This study investigated how gender and personality interact in natural language expression using XAI techniques.

Our findings suggest that (1) the model and the attribution outputs capture clear gender-typical content, consistent with prior work on gender differences in language; (2) trait-specific differences within each gender could be identified only tentatively, with no clear pattern for Agreeableness; and (3) attribution-based explainability can surface such patterns for qualitative inspection, although it does not by itself establish them.

The qualitative observations discussed below come from attribution-selected texts (see Phase 3: Selection and Interpretation of Attribution Outputs); because the final reading involves researcher judgment and the examples were neither systematically coded nor statistically tested, we present them as illustrative, candidate patterns rather than established effects.
The word attribution analysis shows clear genderspecific patterns that are consistent with previous findings (Mehl et al., 2006; Park et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The word attribution analysis shows clear genderspecific patterns that are consistent with previous findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Mehl et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Park et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The highest-attribution words mainly reflect what men and women write about rather than how they write it.

Both lists combine relationship terms, which reflect gendered referents ("girlfriend" for males, "boyfriend" for females), with terms for social and leisure settings ("roommate" and "band" for males, "sorority" and "dance" for females), and they differ more in the particular settings mentioned than in kind; positive evaluation ("cute") also appears among the female words.

While prior research has identified broad distinctions in male and female language (Newman et al., 2008; Tackman et al., 2020), our trait-level analyses suggest that these distinctions vary somewhat within each gender.
text.formatted: While prior research has identified broad distinctions in male and female language <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Newman et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al., 2020)</ref>, our trait-level analyses suggest that these distinctions vary somewhat within each gender.

text.text: The whole-text reading suggested patterns that fit the content of the traits (Table 4): reappraisal of distress at low Neuroticism in both genders, with irritation among men and worry among women at high Neuroticism; laziness versus work completion among men at the two ends of Conscientiousness; shyness among low-Extraversion women; and abstract reflections among high-Openness men.
These patterns are in line with earlier evidence that personality is expressed in language (Mehl et al., 2006; Tackman et al., 2020).
text.formatted: These patterns are in line with earlier evidence that personality is expressed in language <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Mehl et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Across trait levels, however, the attribution outputs were dominated by the same gender-typical content found in the gender-only analysis, so whether and how trait level modulates gendered language remains open and would require larger samples and designs built for the interaction.
Comparison With Earlier Findings.

Some of our observations can be compared with earlier work, although our written, stream-of-consciousness data are a reasonable but not equivalent basis for comparison with the spoken-language studies of Mehl et al. (2006) and Tackman et al. (2020). Newman et al. (2008) found a small gender difference in the use of discrepancy words (e.g., "should", "would", "could"), with women using them slightly more than men (d = 0.07).

These examples cannot show that the small aggregate difference reflects different communicative functions, but they suggest that attribution-based reading can complement word counts.

Similarly, the intensive adverb "really", which women used more than men in the whole sample, in line with Park et al. (2016), remained significant among participants low in Neuroticism but not among those high in it.
