Overall Pattern.

These comparisons are mixed: the gender-typical content and the low-Extraversion pattern are consistent with earlier research (Mehl et al., 2006; Tackman et al., 2020), whereas the sexual-language and Agreeableness results are not.
text.formatted: These comparisons are mixed: the gender-typical content and the low-Extraversion pattern are consistent with earlier research <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Mehl et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al., 2020)</ref>, whereas the sexual-language and Agreeableness results are not.

text.text: The classifier's balanced accuracy (0.815) is well above chance but far from perfect, so these differences should be read as tendencies in the text fragments rather than a clean separation between men's and women's writing.
What Attribution Adds.
Our use of XAI techniques, in particular BERT with integrated gradients, shows which words drive the classifier's predictions for each gender and trait group.

This method identifies specific words and phrases that influence model predictions, providing insight into how BERT makes decisions about gender by attributing importance to specific linguistic features (Sundararajan et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This method identifies specific words and phrases that influence model predictions, providing insight into how BERT makes decisions about gender by attributing importance to specific linguistic features <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Sundararajan et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: A bottom-up analysis can detect variables and interactions that were not specified in advance (Boyd & Markowitz, 2024).
text.formatted: A bottom-up analysis can detect variables and interactions that were not specified in advance <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Boyd & Markowitz, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our results are consistent with the ability of XAI to surface patterns that align with theoretical frameworks, but they do not by themselves validate the method.
Compared with TF-IDF and logistic regression, the main difference is contextual sensitivity.

Unlike bag-of-words methods that treat each word as an isolated unit with fixed importance regardless of surrounding text, BERT generates contextualized embeddings where the same word receives different representations depending on its linguistic environment (Devlin et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Unlike bag-of-words methods that treat each word as an isolated unit with fixed importance regardless of surrounding text, BERT generates contextualized embeddings where the same word receives different representations depending on its linguistic environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Devlin et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, as reported in the Results, for several male words (e.g., "stream", "roommate", "love") the word itself received attribution near zero and its selection mainly reflected the surrounding essay, a distinction that a fixed perword weight in bag-of-words approaches cannot capture.
More broadly, the attribution outputs suggest that the model's decisions are not limited to a few gendered words, since the attribution-selected texts also contain topical and emotional content.
Classification performance should be read with the same caution.
A balanced accuracy of 0.815 shows that the model detects gender-related signal in the essays, but not what that signal consists of.
Attribution outputs make it possible to check whether the words driving the predictions are consistent with prior theory.
In our data they partly are: the highest-attribution words reflect relationship, social, and leisure content, whereas trait-specific differences within each gender were modest and tentative.
High accuracy is therefore a reason to inspect the model, not evidence that it captures theoretically meaningful differences, and attribution methods are what make that inspection possible.
The Data Source.
The stream-of-consciousness format may also capture less self-censored, more spontaneous expression than traditional assessment methods (e.g., questionnaires).

Unlike self-reports, which are vulnerable to social desirability bias, acquiescence, and self-deception (Paulhus & Vazire, 2007), naturalistic language analysis might be less exposed to these biases, as it examines spontaneous verbal expression rather than deliberate self-evaluation.
text.formatted: Unlike self-reports, which are vulnerable to social desirability bias, acquiescence, and self-deception <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Paulhus & Vazire, 2007)</ref>, naturalistic language analysis might be less exposed to these biases, as it examines spontaneous verbal expression rather than deliberate self-evaluation.

text.text: Our methodological framework (Saeteros et al., 2025) combines naturalistic language data with XAI techniques, and their contributions should be kept apart.
text.formatted: Our methodological framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Saeteros et al., 2025)</ref> combines naturalistic language data with XAI techniques, and their contributions should be kept apart.

text.text: The freedom from self-report biases stems from the data source itself, not from the model; what XAI adds is the ability to inspect which words and texts drive the model's predictions for each gender and trait group.

The patterns reported here suggest the potential of this combination to describe fine-grained differences that complement existing measurement methods, and offer a possible template for interpreting complex psychological constructs through theoretically grounded language analysis (Grahek et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The patterns reported here suggest the potential of this combination to describe fine-grained differences that complement existing measurement methods, and offer a possible template for interpreting complex psychological constructs through theoretically grounded language analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Grahek et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Our transformer-based approach with XAI is intended to complement dictionary-based methods.

Methods like LIWC remain useful for hypothesis-driven research where theoretical expectations are clear, offering transparency and replicability, and questionnaires capture aspects of personality expression, such as conscious self-concepts, that behavioral data cannot access.
Contextual embeddings combined with integrated gradients add the possibility of examining context-dependent patterns in language.
Another methodological consideration is the role of gender-identifying terms such as "boyfriend/girlfriend", which might be considered obvious lexical cues.
We retained them for two reasons.
First, previous work on gender-personality interactions in language, including Tackman et al. (2020), treats relationship terms as meaningful indicators of linguistic expression.
text.formatted: First, previous work on gender-personality interactions in language, including <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al. (2020)</ref>, treats relationship terms as meaningful indicators of linguistic expression.

text.text: Second, they appear in only a minority of essays, and masking them left classification performance essentially unchanged (see Results), so the classifier does not depend on them alone.

Moreover, BERT's architecture encode more than lexical choices: as Rogers et al. (2020) document, BERT's multiple layers encode morphological, syntactic, and semantic information through contextualized embeddings.
Integrated gradients allows us to inspect which words drive classification decisions.

In our outputs, the highest-attribution words were mostly content words (e.g., relationship terms, social and leisure settings), with a few function words (e.g., "though", "someone") among the trait-level words.

This differs in emphasis from LIWC-based approaches, which have highlighted function words, sentence length, and other syntactic categories (Newman et al., 2008; Pennebaker et al., 2003; Tackman et al., 2020); because we did not compare predictive power across linguistic levels, we cannot conclude that semantic content is more informative than these categories.
text.formatted: This differs in emphasis from LIWC-based approaches, which have highlighted function words, sentence length, and other syntactic categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Newman et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Pennebaker et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al., 2020)</ref>; because we did not compare predictive power across linguistic levels, we cannot conclude that semantic content is more informative than these categories.

text.text: We urge caution when interpreting our findings, because several questions arise when working with language and ML methods (Van Der Wal et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We urge caution when interpreting our findings, because several questions arise when working with language and ML methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Van Der Wal et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: First, language carries substantial information about the speaker, their self-identification, and membership in socio-demographic groups (Hovy & Prabhumoye, 2021).
text.formatted: First, language carries substantial information about the speaker, their self-identification, and membership in socio-demographic groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hovy & Prabhumoye, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Second, language conveys information about the society the speaker inhabits (Caliskan et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Second, language conveys information about the society the speaker inhabits <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Caliskan et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: With this in mind, it is possible that the results discussed above carry biases present in the data used for our analyses.
By bias, in a strictly probabilistic sense, we refer to a deviation from the expectation we should have for something before we see any further evidence (Hovy & Prabhumoye, 2021).
text.formatted: By bias, in a strictly probabilistic sense, we refer to a deviation from the expectation we should have for something before we see any further evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hovy & Prabhumoye, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In this sample of undergraduate students from the early 2000s, for instance, men are more likely to write "girlfriend" and women "boyfriend" than the reverse.

An alternative explanation for our results could therefore be that we are detecting membership in a socio-demographic group at a certain point in time rather than meaningful linguistic differences between genders.

However, two observations suggest that the model captures signal beyond demographic markers: masking these terms left performance essentially unchanged, and the attribution outputs point to diverse features.
Our findings point to three implications, which we present as directions rather than conclusions.
First, for the study of gender and personality in language, the attribution outputs show that a gender classifier relies heavily on gender-typical content, particularly relationship terms.

The trait-specific patterns that emerged within each gender (Table 4) can be stated as testable gender × trait interactions: (a) at high Neuroticism, negative affect is expressed more as irritation or anger by men and more as worry or anxiety by women, in line with the female-specific association between Neuroticism and sadness words reported by Tackman et al. (2020); (b) Conscientiousness is more strongly associated with references to completing or avoiding work among men than among women; (c) low Extraversion is more strongly associated with references to shyness and loneliness among women than among men; and (d) Openness is more strongly associated with abstract and existential content among men than among women.

(2020)</ref>; (b) Conscientiousness is more strongly associated with references to completing or avoiding work among men than among women; (c) low Extraversion is more strongly associated with references to shyness and loneliness among women than among men; and (d) Openness is more strongly associated with abstract and existential content among men than among women.

text.text: An association between Openness and abstract concepts has been reported in the same corpus without separating by gender (Saeteros et al., 2025), so only the gender-specific part of this prediction is new.
text.formatted: An association between Openness and abstract concepts has been reported in the same corpus without separating by gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Saeteros et al., 2025)</ref>, so only the gender-specific part of this prediction is new.

text.text: Because these hypotheses were derived from the present data, they should be tested in independent corpora.

Second, for language-based personality assessment, Tackman et al. (2020) found genderspecific associations between personality and language, which suggests that models should not assume the same mapping for men and women.
text.formatted: Second, for language-based personality assessment, <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al. (2020)</ref> found genderspecific associations between personality and language, which suggests that models should not assume the same mapping for men and women.

text.text: Our classifier predicted gender, not personality, and masking the relationship terms barely changed its accuracy; whether gendered content affects language-based personality models would need to be tested directly.

Third, attribution-guided reading can surface candidate patterns that broader statistical approaches might miss (Mõttus, 2022), complementing traditional methods that have identified robust patterns (Soto, 2019).

text.text: The same approach could be applied to other longstanding questions in personality and individual differences, such as the relation between personality and culture (Allik et al., 2023).

text.text: Several limitations should be noted.

The most significant is that our sample consists of predominantly Western undergraduate students writing stream-of-consciousness essays in an academic setting, which may have shaped language use and may limit generalization to other age groups, populations and cultural contexts (Costa et al., 2001).
text.formatted: The most significant is that our sample consists of predominantly Western undergraduate students writing stream-of-consciousness essays in an academic setting, which may have shaped language use and may limit generalization to other age groups, populations and cultural contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Costa et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Language also varies across age groups (Hovy & Prabhumoye, 2021), so the patterns identified here may not hold elsewhere.
text.formatted: Language also varies across age groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hovy & Prabhumoye, 2021)</ref>, so the patterns identified here may not hold elsewhere.

text.text: An important limitation concerns the challenge of separating linguistic style from topical content in stream-of-consciousness essays.

Because the instruction did not specify a topic, participants wrote about diverse subjects, creating potential confounds between what people discuss and how they express themselves (e.g., "girlfriend/boyfriend" may indicate relationship focus rather than linguistic style).

Although the masking check and the diversity of attributed features suggest that the patterns are not limited to such content, this cannot be conclusively established without additional datasets collected with different methods.
In addition, the trait groups were defined from global self-report scores, which may partly reflect self-image, identity and gender norms (Buck et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In addition, the trait groups were defined from global self-report scores, which may partly reflect self-image, identity and gender norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Buck et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Males and females with similar scores may therefore not be equivalent in their underlying trait levels, and our trait groups should be read as groups defined by questionnaire scores.
The Big Five items were administered with simplified wording, which may limit comparability with standard BFI scores.

A further limitation concerns the review of the extensive attribution outputs generated by integrated gradients, which produce attribution scores for every word in every text, a volume too large to analyze comprehensively by hand.

We therefore used attribution scores to select the words and texts to read (see Phase 3: Selection and Interpretation of Attribution Outputs), so that selection is driven by the model rather than by the researchers.
The final step of reading and choosing examples nevertheless involves researcher judgment, and our synthesis is illustrative rather than exhaustive.

The reading was done by a single reader without an inter-rater check, the same fragment can be selected in several groups, some high-attribution texts were hard to interpret, and the trait-quartile groups are small, so a few essays can dominate a group.
Future research should pursue three directions.

First, the candidate patterns reported here should be tested for replication across larger samples, age groups, cultures and communication contexts, for instance by applying these XAI techniques to other spontaneous language datasets, such as those used by Tackman et al. (2020) or the Reddit-based PAN-DORA corpus (Gjurković et al., 2021).
text.formatted: First, the candidate patterns reported here should be tested for replication across larger samples, age groups, cultures and communication contexts, for instance by applying these XAI techniques to other spontaneous language datasets, such as those used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Tackman et al. (2020)</ref> or the Reddit-based PAN-DORA corpus <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gjurković et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This is also relevant because recent studies on LLMs, such as Peters and Matz (2024), highlight the potential for demographic biases in psychological profiling, with more accurate personality inferences observed for women compared to men.
text.formatted: This is also relevant because recent studies on LLMs, such as <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Peters and Matz (2024)</ref>, highlight the potential for demographic biases in psychological profiling, with more accurate personality inferences observed for women compared to men.

text.text: Second, controlled designs that hold content constant across participants (e.g., standardized writing prompts) or systematically vary topic assignment would help separate linguistic style from content.

Third, the judgment-based last step of our procedure could be made more objective, for instance by using embedding-based similarity (e.g., cosine similarity between attribution-selected fragments) to group and retrieve texts, and computational methods for synthesizing attribution outputs at scale would make such analyses more comprehensive and reproducible.

Using integrated gradients on a BERT gender classifier, we found that the attribution outputs capture clear gender-typical content, mainly relationship terms and social and leisure settings, in line with prior work.
Within each gender, a few trait-specific patterns emerged, which we state as four testable gender × trait interactions (see Implications) for larger samples and more automated analysis techniques.
Attribution-guided reading thus offers a way to generate hypotheses about how gender and personality are expressed in language, which designs built for the gender-trait interaction can then evaluate.
